text:
Knowing the rules of good design gets you halfway. The other half is a process... for applying them, and for changing a design once it's live. Say an online store wants a database. You could just start typing tables... but then your schema is a first guess. Instead, ask the same questions, in order. Gather requirements. Find the entities, and their facts. Work out how they relate. Pick keys, add constraints, normalize. Then test it with real rows. And when a row breaks it? Loop back, and revise.

Step one is plain sentences. A customer places orders. A product has a name and a price. Categories group products, and a product can sit in several. And an order contains products, each with a quantity... and the price charged. The nouns are your entities. The verbs say how they connect.

Step two makes each noun a table: customers, products, categories, orders. Step three puts each fact on the thing it describes. An email describes a customer. A price describes a product. And an order doesn't copy the customer's email. It points at the customer's row, so each fact lives in one place.

Step four: how many connect to how many? One customer places many orders... and each order has exactly one customer. Products and categories are many on both sides, so they meet in a table of pairs, product categories. Orders and products are many to many, too. But that link has facts of its own: how many, and at what price. So it becomes a real table, order items, one row per line on the receipt.

Step five, keys. Order items is keyed by the pair, so the same product can't land on one order twice. Step six turns rules into constraints. A quantity has to be above zero, so a line for zero mugs... is refused by Postgres itself.
